title: Dual-Mode Propulsion: MIT's Game-Changing Engine Could Unleash Small Satellites on the Solar System
summary:
Spacecraft face a fundamental trade-off: powerful chemical rockets that guzzle fuel for quick maneuvers, or hyper-efficient electric thrusters that sip propellant but can't generate much force. Until now, you needed separate systems with different fuels—adding weight, complexity, and cost. But MIT researchers have found a way to have your cake and eat it too, with a single propulsion system that does both.

The key is a "green monopropellant" called ASCENT, originally developed by the U.S. Air Force for chemical thrusters. The MIT team discovered it also works beautifully in electrospray thrusters—tiny electric engines the size of a dime. These use electric fields to charge and eject ions from the liquid, producing a gentle but incredibly efficient thrust. "If you can have chemical and electrical propulsion in one small package, it's the best of both worlds," says lead author Amelia Bruno. "This opens the door for small satellites to do even more science, more observations, and more interesting missions, all on a smaller and cheaper platform."

The concept is elegantly simple: a single tank of ASCENT feeds both a chemical thruster for rapid acceleration, deceleration, or sudden course changes, and a set of electrospray thrusters for slow, precise adjustments over long interplanetary journeys. This dual-mode capability is a game-changer for small satellites like CubeSats, which are typically limited to low Earth orbit because they lack the propulsion to go farther.

To prove it, the team is collaborating with NASA on the Green Propulsion Dual Mode mission. A briefcase-sized CubeSat will carry one chemical thruster and four electrospray thrusters, all drawing from the same propellant tank. It will be the first in-space test of this dual-mode system on a small spacecraft. If successful, it could open the solar system to a new class of explorers. "We could send CubeSats to Mars, or the asteroid belt, where they could make the journey slowly, using electrospray thrusters," says co-author Paulo Lozano. "You could then use your chemical thrusters to quickly move to look at interesting features."

The implications are enormous. Small satellites are far cheaper to build and launch than traditional large spacecraft. Giving them the ability to travel deep into space and perform complex maneuvers could revolutionize planetary science, asteroid prospecting, and even space weather monitoring. And because ASCENT is non-toxic and stable in the vacuum of space, it's safer and simpler to handle than many traditional propellants. The team's study, published in the Journal of Propulsion and Power, marks a crucial step toward making ambitious small-satellite missions a reality.
why_it_matters: This breakthrough could democratize deep-space exploration, allowing high schools, colleges, or small nations to send probes to asteroids or planets instead of only giant space agencies. For students now, that means the solar system may soon be studied by cheap, flexible swarms of tiny spacecraft, opening countless new discovery opportunities.

background_read: Most rockets today use either chemical thrusters, which burn fuel quickly for big boosts, or electric thrusters, which use electric fields to push out ions slowly but very efficiently.

The monopropellant ASCENT was originally developed by the U.S. Air Force as a safer, non-toxic alternative to hydrazine, a common but hazardous fuel. MIT researchers accidentally discovered it also works well in tiny electrospray engines.

CubeSats are standardized small satellites that have drastically lowered the cost of space research. Until now, they’ve mostly been stuck in low Earth orbit because they lack the propulsive power to reach deeper space.
NASA’s Green Propulsion Dual Mode mission will launch a briefcase-sized CubeSat into deep space to test this combined system for the first time.
If successful, this technology could let university or small-company satellites explore asteroids, moons, and planets on modest budgets.

perspectives.description: Combining two propulsion modes in one compact package drastically reduces satellite mass and cost. This lets small spacecraft leave low Earth orbit for the first time, enabling ambitious science missions that were once only possible with large, expensive probes. It also simplifies launch logistics because ASCENT is safer to load and handle.

A single-propellant dual-mode system creates a single point of failure: if the fuel tank leaks, both thruster types are lost. Additionally, electrospray thrusters are still relatively new in spaceflight, and their long-term reliability in deep-space environments is unproven. Overconfidence in cheap CubeSats could lead to lost missions and space debris.

This dual-mode approach reflects a broader trend toward reconfigurable spacecraft. By using one fuel for two very different engine types, engineers trade peak performance for adaptability — an elegant solution for mass-constrained missions. However, it requires sophisticated software to manage transitions between power-hungry chemical burns and slow electric cruises.

If CubeSats can reach the asteroid belt, space resource prospecting and sample-return missions could become affordable for private companies. This might accelerate both scientific discovery and commercial mining, raising urgent questions about planetary protection and ownership rights. The technology may also inspire a new generation of student-built interplanetary projects.
